rows.solution:
Test each description in turn against \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & -5 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 4{\cdot}3 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).
Skew-symmetric would require \(A' = -A\), which forces every diagonal entry to be \(0\); here \(a_{22} = 3 \ne 0\), and in any case \(a_{13} = -5\) while \(a_{31} = 4{\cdot}3 \ne 5\). So it is not skew-symmetric.
Diagonal would require every entry off the leading diagonal to be \(0\), but \(a_{13} = -5\) and \(a_{31} = 4{\cdot}3\) are non-zero. So it is not diagonal, and a scalar matrix — a diagonal matrix with all its diagonal entries equal — is ruled out for the same reason.
What is left is simply the order: A has \(3\) rows and \(3\) columns, so it is a square matrix.

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.figure: REQUIRED — the question IS the printed graph; the stem names no curve at all. Two branches opening left and right, drawn only for \(|x| \ge 1\), with the Y-axis marked \(-\pi, -\pi/2, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2, 2\pi\) and dashed horizontal lines at \(y = -\pi/2\), \(y = \pi/2\) and \(y = 3\pi/2\). Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
Read the picture rather than looking for a formula.
The curve is drawn only for \(|x| \ge 1\) — nothing at all is plotted between \(x = -1\) and \(x = 1\) — and all of its asymptotes are HORIZONTAL (the dashed lines \(y = -\frac{\pi}{2}\), \(y = \frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(y = \frac{3\pi}{2}\)). Both \(y = \sec x\) and \(y = \text{cosec}\, x\) are periodic in \(x\) with VERTICAL asymptotes and take every value with \(|y| \ge 1\), so neither can be this graph; also their domain gaps run along the y-direction, not a solid block \(-1 < x < 1\) of the x-axis. That leaves the two inverse functions, and a domain of \(|x| \ge 1\) fits both of them.
The deciding feature is where each branch turns. The right-hand branch has its vertex ON the x-axis at \((1, 0)\), and \(\sec^{-1}(1) = 0\) whereas \(\text{cosec}^{-1}(1) = \frac{\pi}{2}\); correspondingly the left-hand branch turns at \((-1, \pi)\), and \(\sec^{-1}(-1) = \pi\). The asymptote \(y = \frac{\pi}{2}\) is exactly the value \(\sec^{-1} x\) approaches as \(|x| \to \infty\) (the branches above and below are the same curve shifted by multiples of \(\pi\)).
Hence the graph depicts \(y = \sec^{-1} x\).

rows.stem: \(f(x) = x^x\) has a critical point at :
rows.solution:
A critical point is a point of the domain where \(f'(x) = 0\) or \(f'\) fails to exist. The domain of \(f(x) = x^x\) is \(x > 0\), so \(x = 0\) is not even in the domain and cannot be a critical point.
Differentiate logarithmically. Let \(y = x^x\); taking logarithms, \(\log y = x \log x\). Differentiating both sides with respect to x,
\(\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = \log x + x \cdot \frac{1}{x} = \log x + 1\),
so
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = x^x\left(1 + \log x\right)\).
Since \(x^x > 0\) for every \(x > 0\), the derivative vanishes only when
\(1 + \log x = 0 \Rightarrow \log x = -1 \Rightarrow x = e^{-1}\).
Hence the critical point is \(x = e^{-1}\). (At \(x = e\) the derivative is \(e^{e}(1 + 1) = 2e^{e} \ne 0\), and at \(x = 1\) it is \(1(1 + 0) = 1 \ne 0\), so neither of those is critical.)

rows.subtopic: Order and Degree of a Differential Equation
rows.stem: The order and degree of the differential equation \(\left[\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} - 1\right]^2 = \dfrac{dy}{dx}\) are, respectively :
rows.solution:
The ORDER is the order of the highest derivative present. Here the highest is \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), so the order is \(2\).
For the DEGREE, the equation must first be a polynomial in the derivatives — and this one already is, once the bracket is expanded:
\(\left[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} - 1\right]^2 = \frac{dy}{dx} \Rightarrow \left(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^2 - 2\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + 1 - \frac{dy}{dx} = 0\).
No derivative sits inside a logarithm, a radical or a trigonometric function, so the degree is defined, and it is the power to which the HIGHEST derivative is raised, namely \(2\).
Hence the order and degree are respectively '2, 2'.

rows.stem: A meeting will be held only if all three members A, B and C are present. The probability that member A does not turn up is \(0{\cdot}10\), member B does not turn up is \(0{\cdot}20\) and member C does not turn up is \(0{\cdot}05\). The probability of the meeting being cancelled is :
rows.solution:
The meeting is held only if ALL THREE members turn up, so it is cancelled precisely when at least one of them is absent. Work with the complement.
The probabilities that the members DO turn up are
\(P(A) = 1 - 0\cdot10 = 0\cdot90\), \(P(B) = 1 - 0\cdot20 = 0\cdot80\), \(P(C) = 1 - 0\cdot05 = 0\cdot95\),
and, taking the three attendances to be independent,
\(P(\text{meeting held}) = 0\cdot90 \times 0\cdot80 \times 0\cdot95 = 0\cdot684\).
Therefore
\(P(\text{meeting cancelled}) = 1 - 0\cdot684 = 0\cdot316\),
which is the choice \(0\cdot316\).
(The value \(0\cdot35\) is what you get by simply adding \(0\cdot10 + 0\cdot20 + 0\cdot05\), which over-counts the overlaps; \(0\cdot001\) is the probability that all three are absent.)

rows.stem: Find the interval in which \(f(x) = x + \dfrac{1}{x}\) is always increasing, \(x \ne 0\).

Find the angle at which the given lines are inclined to each other :

\(l_1 : \dfrac{x - 5}{2} = \dfrac{y + 3}{1} = \dfrac{z - 1}{-3}\)

\(l_2 : \dfrac{x}{3} = \dfrac{y - 1}{2} = \dfrac{z + 5}{-1}\)
rows.solution:
Both lines are already in symmetric form, so their direction ratios can be read straight off:
\(l_1\) has direction ratios \((2, 1, -3)\) and \(l_2\) has direction ratios \((3, 2, -1)\).
If \(\theta\) is the angle between the lines, then
\(\cos\theta = \frac{|a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2|}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2}\ \sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2}}\).
The numerator is
\((2)(3) + (1)(2) + (-3)(-1) = 6 + 2 + 3 = 11\),
and each magnitude is
\(\sqrt{2^2 + 1^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{14}\), \(\sqrt{3^2 + 2^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{14}\).
Hence
\(\cos\theta = \frac{11}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{14}} = \frac{11}{14}\), so \(\theta = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{11}{14}\right)\)
(about \(38^{\circ}13'\)). Note that the points \((5, -3, 1)\) and \((0, 1, -5)\) on the lines play no part — the angle between two lines depends only on their directions.

rows.stem: Find the value of x, if \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & x & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 \\ 15 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ x \end{bmatrix} = O.\)
rows.solution:
Multiply from the right, so that every intermediate step stays a single column. First,
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 \\ 15 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ x \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 6 + 2x \\ 2 + 10 + x \\ 15 + 6 + 2x \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 + 2x \\ 12 + x \\ 21 + 2x \end{bmatrix}\).
Now pre-multiply by the row matrix:
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & x & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 7 + 2x \\ 12 + x \\ 21 + 2x \end{bmatrix} = (7 + 2x) + x(12 + x) + (21 + 2x)\)
\(= 7 + 2x + 12x + x^2 + 21 + 2x = x^2 + 16x + 28\).
The product is the \(1 \times 1\) zero matrix, so
\(x^2 + 16x + 28 = 0 \Rightarrow (x + 14)(x + 2) = 0\)
(since \(14 \times 2 = 28\) and \(14 + 2 = 16\)).
Hence \(x = -14\) or \(x = -2\). Both roots are admissible — nothing in the question excludes either.

rows.stem: Bag I contains 4 white and 5 black balls. Bag II contains 6 white and 7 black balls. A ball drawn randomly by from bag I is transferred to bag II and then a ball is drawn randomly from bag II. Find the probability that the ball drawn is white.
rows.solution:
The colour of the transferred ball is not known, so the two possibilities must be taken separately and their contributions added: this is the theorem of total probability.
Bag I holds \(4 + 5 = 9\) balls, so
\(P(\text{white transferred}) = \frac{4}{9}\), \(P(\text{black transferred}) = \frac{5}{9}\).
Bag II starts with \(6\) white and \(7\) black, i.e. \(13\) balls, and the transfer makes it \(14\).
If a WHITE ball was transferred, Bag II holds \(7\) white out of \(14\), so the conditional probability of drawing white is \(\frac{7}{14}\).
If a BLACK ball was transferred, Bag II holds \(6\) white out of \(14\), so the conditional probability is \(\frac{6}{14}\).
Therefore
\(P(\text{white drawn}) = \frac{4}{9} \cdot \frac{7}{14} + \frac{5}{9} \cdot \frac{6}{14} = \frac{28}{126} + \frac{30}{126} = \frac{58}{126} = \frac{29}{63}\).
So the probability that the ball drawn from Bag II is white is \(\frac{29}{63}\), which is about \(0\cdot460\).

rows.subtopic: Area Bounded by a Curve and a Line
rows.stem: Using integration, find the area of the ellipse \(\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\) bounded between the lines \(x = -\dfrac{a}{2}\) to \(x = \dfrac{a}{2}\).
rows.solution:
The ellipse \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\) is symmetric about BOTH axes, and the strip cut off between \(x = -\frac{a}{2}\) and \(x = \frac{a}{2}\) shares that symmetry, so it is enough to work out the part lying in the first quadrant and multiply by \(4\).
Solving for the upper half, \(y = \frac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\). Hence
\(\text{Area} = 4\int_{0}^{a/2} \frac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\;dx = \frac{4b}{a}\int_{0}^{a/2} \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\;dx\).
Using the standard result \(\int \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\,dx = \frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \frac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a}\),
\(\text{Area} = \frac{4b}{a}\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \frac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a}\right]_{0}^{a/2}\).
At the upper limit \(x = \frac{a}{2}\) we have \(\sqrt{a^2 - \frac{a^2}{4}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}\,a}{2}\) and \(\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{6}\); the lower limit contributes nothing. So
\(\text{Area} = \frac{4b}{a}\left[\frac{a}{4}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}\,a}{2} + \frac{a^2}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{6}\right] = \frac{4b}{a}\left[\frac{\sqrt{3}\,a^2}{8} + \frac{\pi a^2}{12}\right]\)
\(= ab\left[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{\pi}{3}\right]\) square units.
As a check this is roughly \(1\cdot913\,ab\), about \(61\%\) of the whole ellipse \(\pi ab \approx 3\cdot142\,ab\), which is the right sort of share for the middle half of the width.

rows.stem: Show that the line passing through the points \(A(0,\ -1,\ -1)\) and \(B(4,\ 5,\ 1)\) intersects the line joining points \(C(3,\ 9,\ 4)\) and \(D(-4,\ 4,\ 4)\).
rows.solution:
Two lines in space meet if and only if they are COPLANAR and not parallel, so both conditions have to be checked.
The line through \(A(0, -1, -1)\) and \(B(4, 5, 1)\) has direction ratios
\(\langle 4 - 0,\ 5 + 1,\ 1 + 1 \rangle = \langle 4, 6, 2 \rangle\),
and the line through \(C(3, 9, 4)\) and \(D(-4, 4, 4)\) has direction ratios
\(\langle -4 - 3,\ 4 - 9,\ 4 - 4 \rangle = \langle -7, -5, 0 \rangle\).
For coplanarity of the lines through \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2, z_2)\) with those directions, the condition is
\(\begin{vmatrix} x_2 - x_1 & y_2 - y_1 & z_2 - z_1 \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{vmatrix} = 0\).
Taking \(A\) and \(C\) as the two points,
\(\begin{vmatrix} 3 - 0 & 9 + 1 & 4 + 1 \\ 4 & 6 & 2 \\ -7 & -5 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 10 & 5 \\ 4 & 6 & 2 \\ -7 & -5 & 0 \end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 3\left(6 \cdot 0 - 2 \cdot (-5)\right) - 10\left(4 \cdot 0 - 2 \cdot (-7)\right) + 5\left(4 \cdot (-5) - 6 \cdot (-7)\right)\)
\(= 3(10) - 10(14) + 5(22) = 30 - 140 + 110 = 0\).
So the two lines are coplanar. They are also not parallel, since \(\langle 4, 6, 2 \rangle\) and \(\langle -7, -5, 0 \rangle\) are not proportional (for instance \(c_1 = 2 \ne 0 = c_2\) while \(a_1, a_2\) are both non-zero). Two coplanar lines that are not parallel must meet, so the line AB does intersect the line CD.
The point of intersection is easy to locate: a point of AB is \((4t,\ -1 + 6t,\ -1 + 2t)\) and every point of CD has \(z = 4\), so \(-1 + 2t = 4\) gives \(t = \frac{5}{2}\) and the point \((10, 14, 4)\). This does lie on CD, since \((10, 14, 4) = C + (-1)\langle -7, -5, 0 \rangle = (3 + 7,\ 9 + 5,\ 4)\).
[Note: the marking scheme stops at the vanishing determinant and writes 'Hence lines intersect each other'. A zero determinant on its own only establishes that the lines are coplanar — coplanar lines may instead be parallel — so the short check that the direction ratios are not proportional, shown above, is what completes the argument. The scheme's conclusion is correct.]
